title: Srivijaya: The Sea Kingdom of the Malay World

cards.h: A sea empire with no mountains
cards.b:
Srivijaya was a kingdom based on the sea. From about the 600s to the 1200s it grew rich by controlling the trade through the straits between Sumatra and Malaya. Its ships carried goods from China, India and the Arab world.

Few people in the West have heard of Srivijaya. It shows how much of the early world's history was written by water, not just by land.

cards.h: A king with twenty thousand soldiers
cards.b:
An inscription dated 683 CE, found near Palembang on Sumatra, is one of the earliest Malay texts. It describes a king who set out by boat with a large army. The text speaks of about twenty thousand men, a figure that shows the scale of the power.

Palembang sits on the Musi river. From there the rulers controlled routes into the interior and the straits, and they charged tolls on ships.

Srivijaya grew rich from port fees and taxes on trade. Ships from China, India and the Arab world called at its ports. The rulers kept order on the sea and offered protection to merchants.

Goods such as camphor, spices, gold, ceramics and aromatic woods passed through. The kingdom was less a single state than a web of ports under one ruler's protection.

Yijing (I-Ching), a Chinese Buddhist monk (671–695)

On his way to India, Yijing stopped at Srivijaya. He wrote that more than a thousand Buddhist monks studied there. He advised monks to learn Sanskrit grammar and prepare for India by staying in Srivijaya first.

His account is one of the best sources for the kingdom's role as a centre of learning.
Srivijaya reached its peak in the 7th to 11th centuries. Its decline came with new rivals, and its trade moved to other ports.

cards.h: The Buddhist centre of the sea
cards.b:
Srivijaya was a major Buddhist centre. Monks studied Sanskrit texts and taught in its monasteries. It was a place where scholars from China, India and the Malay world met and debated.

Its teachers were respected across Asia. The Mahayana tradition was strong, and the kingdom sent students and teachers out to other places in the region.

Many modern books describe Srivijaya as a great empire, with a capital and a clear territory. The image is simple and easy to teach.

Historians argue it was closer to a network of allied ports, linked by trade and by the power of one ruling family. Some use the older word "mandala" to describe such a loose state. The debate matters for how we tell Southeast Asian history.

Ships in this trade were moved by the monsoon winds. The winds blew one way in one season and the other way in the next. Merchants had to wait for months in port for the right wind.

So ports were not just places of trade. They were places of waiting, storage and social life. Srivijaya made money from its ports because it controlled the timing of ships as well as their routes.

In about 1025 the Chola king Rajendra I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal and attacked Srivijaya's ports. The raid showed that sea power was contested and that rival states could strike far away.

The attack did not end Srivijaya, but it weakened its grip on the trade. In the following centuries new states, like Malacca, rose to take over the straits.

Old Malay, used in Srivijaya's inscriptions, became the lingua franca of the trade routes of Southeast Asia. Later, Malay spread along the coasts and became a language of trade, faith and government.

Today Malay and Indonesian are close, and their roots include Srivijaya's world of ports. The language is one of the quiet legacies of a sea empire.

In about 1011 the Indian scholar Atisha, also called Dipankara Srijnana, travelled to Srivijaya. He studied for more than a decade with the Buddhist master Dharmakirti there, learning the teachings and the discipline of the monk.

Atisha later went to Tibet, where his teachings shaped a major Buddhist tradition. The kingdom was a bridge between India and the Tibetan world, carrying ideas as well as goods.

Five things to remember
  1. Srivijaya grew rich from the straits between Sumatra and Malaya.
  2. The 683 inscription comes from Palembang.
  3. Yijing praised its Buddhist learning around 671–695.
  4. The Chola raid of about 1025 hit its ports.
  5. Historians debate whether it was an empire or a network.
Think about it
  • How does sea power differ from land power?
  • Why did the monsoon shape the rise and fall of ports?
